newsitem.title: TURKEY: Kurdish chief to meet U.S. envoy in Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish chief to meet U.S. envoy in Turkey.

text.p: Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani, whose forces took control of north Iraq last week with backing from Baghdad, plans to tell the United States he is not interested in further deals with Iraq, a spokesman for Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) said on Tuesday.

London-based spokesman Dilshad Miran said that Barzani, who is expected to meet with a senior U.S. official on Thursday in Turkey, would also ask that the U.S.-led allied air operation to protect northern Iraq from Baghdad's troops be continued.
"We do not have any other deals with (Iraqi President Saddam Hussein) and that is really our message to the Americans," Miran told Reuters by telephone.
"It was a one-off deal with the Iraqi government," he said.
The U.S. State Department confirmed that a meeting would be held on Thursday between Barzani and Robert Pelletreau, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs.
The State Department did not say where the meeting would take place but the Kurdish group said the talks would be held in Turkey, likely in Ankara or the town of Silopi near the Iraqi border.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States also wanted to arrange negotiations between Barzani and Jalal Talabani, whose Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) was routed this month from its northern Iraq strongholds by KDP forces.
Barzani's forces conquered most of the Kurdish region in fighting with the rival militia after Baghdad's forces helped the KDP take the main regional city of Arbil from the PUK.

The clashes shattered a U.S.-brokered ceasefire between the rival Kurdish factions and boosted Saddam in an area that has been out of his control since a Western no-fly zone was imposed over northern Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War.

Barzani's group says it was forced to ask for Baghdad's help to counter Iranian support for the rival group. The KDP complains that Washington did not do enough to help implement a tentative peace deal between the Kurds agreed last year.
"We need some clear answers. Over the years we have been asking the Americans, the State Department, what their policies are on the Kurdish issue," Miran said.
Iraq's armed support for the KDP on August 31 prompted U.S. missile strikes on Iraq and led to a rapid escalation of tension in the Gulf.

The United States, which sent Stealth fighter-bombers to the region and additional aircraft carriers, threatened further attacks after Iraqi forces shot at Western planes patrolling the "no-fly" zones off-limits to Iraqi aircraft.

The United States has also said it will send 3,500 additional ground forces to Kuwait, one of the world's largest oil exporters. It was overrun by Iraqi troops in 1990, an invasion triggered the 1991 Gulf War.
But a new U.S. attack on Iraq appeared uncertain in the face of Baghdad's retreat from confrontation and a dearth of diplomatic support for President Bill Clinton's tough line toward Saddam.
